title: Punycode: A Bootstring encoding of Unicode for Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA)
subtitle: How a domain label in any script is squeezed into letters, digits and hyphens.
summary: Punycode is a reversible way to write any Unicode string using only the ASCII letters, digits and hyphen that domain name labels allow. It is a particular setting of a general algorithm called Bootstring, tuned for Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA). Plain ASCII characters are copied as they are, and every other character is described compactly by its value and its position.

questions: how do internationalized domain names work
what does xn-- mean in a domain name
how do you convert unicode to punycode
why are domain labels limited to ascii

tldr.problem: Domain labels may contain only letters, digits and hyphens and are limited to 63 characters, yet people want names in every script.
tldr.mechanism: Copy the ASCII characters first, add a hyphen, then encode each remaining character as a position delta in a compact, self-delimiting base-36 number whose size adapts as it goes.
tldr.outcome: Every Unicode label maps to exactly one short ASCII label and back again, so IDNA works over the unchanged DNS.

today: Internationalized domain names are carried in the DNS in their Punycode form. Names such as xn--bcher-kva are the ACE form of bücher, and tools show you one or the other. The modern IDNA specification, RFC 5891, still relies on Punycode, and the algorithm is implemented in the standard library or core libraries of most programming languages and browsers.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Domain Name System was built around names made of ASCII letters, digits and hyphens. The IDNA architecture lets people use other scripts anyway: a label containing non-ASCII characters is represented by an ACE label, which begins with a special ACE prefix and contains only ASCII characters. The part after the prefix is a Punycode encoding of the original Unicode string. The prefix itself and the rules about which strings are allowed belong to IDNA and Nameprep, not to this document.

RFC 3492 defines two things. The first is Bootstring, a general algorithm that lets a string of "basic" code points uniquely represent any string of code points drawn from a larger set. The second is Punycode, which is simply Bootstring with a particular set of parameter values chosen for IDNA.

The RFC is explicit that Punycode "is not designed for any other purpose" than converting domain labels into ASCII, and that it is "explicitly not designed for processing arbitrary free text."
sections.plainLanguage: The Domain Name System was built for names made of ASCII letters, digits and hyphens. IDNA lets people use other scripts by representing such a label as an ASCII string with a special prefix, followed by a Punycode encoding of the original text. This RFC defines Bootstring, a general algorithm, and Punycode, Bootstring with parameters chosen for IDNA. It is not designed for any other purpose.

sections.title: Design goals
sections.content:
The RFC lists six features that Bootstring is meant to have. They pull against each other, and the algorithm tries to balance them.

Completeness
Every string of arbitrary code points can be represented by a string of basic code points.
Uniqueness
There is at most one basic string for a given extended string.
Reversibility
Any extended string that was mapped to a basic string can be recovered from it.
Efficient encoding
The output stays short, which matters because RFC 1034 limits a domain label to 63 characters.
Simplicity
Encoding and decoding should be easy to implement. Simplicity and efficiency are "at odds", so Bootstring aims for a good balance.
Readability
Basic characters that appear in the input are kept as themselves in the output.

Uniqueness matters most for security. If one Unicode label could encode to several ASCII labels, one name could point at several different owners. The unique mapping is what lets DNS keep its promise that a name has a single controlling authority.
sections.plainLanguage: Bootstring has six goals: complete (any string can be represented), unique (each string has one encoding), reversible, short, simple and readable. Some goals conflict, such as simplicity and short output. Uniqueness matters most for security. If one Unicode label could encode to several ASCII labels, one name could point at several different owners.

sections.title: How the encoding works
sections.content:
Bootstring uses three ideas together, followed by a fourth that tunes them.

Basic code point segregation. All basic code points in the input are copied to the start of the output in their original order, followed by a delimiter if, and only if, there is at least one of them. The delimiter never appears in the rest of the output, so a decoder finds the literal portion by looking for the last delimiter.

Insertion unsort coding. The rest of the output is a list of nonnegative numbers called deltas. The decoder starts with the literal portion and inserts the non-basic code points one at a time. It keeps two state variables, a counter n (the code point value being placed) and an index i (a position in the string so far). Each step advances i, and when it passes the end it wraps to 0 and n goes up by one. A delta counts how many positions to skip before the next insertion. Because code points are processed in increasing numeric order rather than in order of appearance, the deltas tend to be small.

Variable-length integers and bias adaptation. The deltas are written as generalized variable-length integers, described in the next section, and a bias value is updated after every delta to keep them short.
sections.plainLanguage: The encoding first copies all basic (ASCII) characters to the start of the output in order, followed by a delimiter if there is at least one. The remaining characters are then described by a list of numbers that say where to insert each one, in increasing order of character value. This keeps the numbers small. The numbers are written as variable-length integers.

sections.title: Variable-length integers and bias
sections.content:
A normal base-36 number is wasteful here because it has no built-in end marker, so numbers glued together would be ambiguous. Punycode instead uses generalized variable-length integers. Digits still run from 0 to base minus 1, but each position j has a threshold t(j). The number ends at the first digit that is less than its threshold, which makes every integer self-delimiting and gives each value exactly one representation. Digits are written least significant first (little-endian), so deltas can be separated starting with the first.

The thresholds are t(j) = base * (j + 1) - bias, clamped between tmin and tmax. The weights follow w(0) = 1 and w(j) = w(j-1) * (base - t(j-1)).

After each delta, adapt() recomputes the bias. The delta is divided by 2 (by damp for the very first one, because the second delta is usually much smaller), increased by delta div numpoints because the next insertion is into a longer string, and repeatedly divided by base - tmin until it is small enough. The bias is then set from the number of divisions and a final term using skew. In effect, the size of the current delta predicts how many digits the next one needs.

The five tuning parameters other than the base affect only efficiency, not correctness. The RFC says they are "best chosen empirically."
sections.plainLanguage: Punycode writes each number as a variable-length integer that marks its own end. Each digit position has a threshold, and the number ends at the first digit below it. Digits are written least significant first. After each number, a bias value is recomputed so the next number is likely to need few digits. Only efficiency, not correctness, depends on the tuning parameters.

sections.title: Parameter values for Punycode
sections.content:
Punycode fixes the Bootstring parameters as shown in the table below. They are designed to suit Unicode code points, which range over 0 to 10FFFF (excluding the UTF-16 surrogates D800 to DFFF), though the only formal restriction is that inputs are nonnegative integers.

The basic code points are the ASCII code points 0 to 7F. The hyphen-minus U+002D is the delimiter. Digit values are assigned like this: the letters A to Z and a to z both stand for 0 to 25, and the digits 0 to 9 stand for 26 to 35. Because initial_n is 128, it is above every basic code point, so the encoder and decoder can skip several checks that general Bootstring needs.

A decoder MUST accept uppercase, lowercase and mixed-case letters. An encoder SHOULD output only one case, unless it uses the optional mixed-case annotation of Appendix A, which is not used by the IDNA ToASCII and ToUnicode operations.

Using the hyphen as the delimiter means an encoded string can end with a hyphen only if the original consisted entirely of basic code points, and IDNA forbids encoding such strings. That keeps labels consistent with the RFC 952 rule that host name labels do not begin or end with a hyphen.

The RFC also warns that people who type encoded strings by hand should watch for look-alike characters such as I, l and 1, or O and 0.
sections.plainLanguage: Punycode fixes the Bootstring parameters. The basic characters are ASCII, and the hyphen is the delimiter. The letters A to Z, in either case, stand for 0 to 25, and the digits 0 to 9 stand for 26 to 35. A decoder must accept any mix of upper and lower case. People typing encoded strings by hand should watch for look-alike characters such as I, l and 1.

sections.title: Algorithms and a worked example
sections.content:
Section 6 gives the algorithms as pseudocode: adapt(), a decoding procedure and an encoding procedure. The decoder fails on invalid code points, unexpected end of input, arithmetic overflow, and any case where a basic code point is encoded as a delta rather than appearing literally. Because it fails in those cases, it cannot produce the same output for two different inputs, so there is no need to re-encode and compare. The encoder repeatedly picks the smallest code point not yet handled, adds (m - n) * (h + 1) to the running delta, counts a step for every earlier character, and writes the delta when it reaches the code point.

Overflow needs care. The RFC says 26-bit unsigned integers are enough for every valid IDNA label, but overflow must still be handled because inputs are not necessarily valid labels.

Take bücher. The basic code points bcher are copied, then a hyphen. The only other code point is ü, U+00FC (252). With n = 128 and h = 5 basic points, delta = (252 - 128) * (5 + 1) = 744, plus 1 for the b that precedes ü, giving 745. With bias 72 and thresholds of 1, 1 and 26, the digits are 10, 21, 0, which are k, v and a. The result is bcher-kva, and IDNA's ACE prefix turns this into xn--bcher-kva.
sections.plainLanguage: This section gives the algorithms as pseudocode for encoding and decoding. The decoder fails on invalid characters, unexpected end of input and arithmetic overflow, so two different inputs cannot give the same output. For example, the German word bücher becomes bcher-kva, and IDNA adds its prefix to give xn--bcher-kva.

sections.title: Security considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's security section is short and about one risk: ambiguity. Users expect each domain name to be controlled by a single authority. If a Unicode string could map to several ACE labels, one internationalized name could correspond to several ASCII domain names, each controlled by a different party, "some of which could be spoofs that hijack service requests intended for another." For that reason Punycode is designed so that each Unicode string has a unique encoding.

That does not solve every problem. There can still be several Unicode representations of the "same" text, "for various definitions of 'same'." The RFC points to the Unicode standard's canonicalization work, which domain names leverage through Nameprep (RFC 3491, the stringprep profile of IDNA at the time).

Punycode only guarantees one encoding per Unicode string. It does not decide whether two different-looking strings are the same text. Preventing confusable names is the job of higher layers.
sections.plainLanguage: The security risk is ambiguity. People expect each domain name to be controlled by one authority. If a Unicode string could map to several ASCII labels, one name could correspond to several domain names, some of them spoofs. Punycode therefore gives each Unicode string a unique encoding. It does not decide whether two different-looking strings are the same text. Higher layers must handle confusable names.

items.title: Basic code point segregation

items.title: Insertion unsort coding
items.text: Other characters are inserted by numeric order, each described by a delta of positions.

items.title: Variable-length integers
items.text: Deltas are little-endian base-36 numbers that end at the first digit below a threshold.

items.title: Bias adaptation
items.text: After each delta the thresholds shift, so a delta of similar size needs fewer digits.
